- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.

- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.

- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.

- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files and comment-only changes.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Claudinite work-item executor (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §6, §10) — a pull worker
# over the queue. ONE RUN PERFORMS ONE ITEM (§15.22), and the queue drains as a
# chain of runs: the scheduler run dispatches this workflow every hour, a run that settled
# its item dispatches the next, and the continuation job below covers a run that
# died before it could. It carries NO cron of its own — the scheduler run's hourly dispatch
# is the guaranteed delivery, so a lost `task:ready` label event is latency lost
# and never work lost.
#
# THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE SECRETS LIVE (DESIGN §14). The wiring converge stamps
# every task's declared `required_secrets`, plus each configured invocation
# endpoint's token secret, into the step env below by name — the scheduler run and the
# janitor get none, because they never execute task code. Code-work is the only task
# code that ever sees a value; the agent hop carries nothing.
#
# MORE CAPACITY IS MORE EXECUTORS. Nothing enumerates them and each claim is
# independently leased, so a second job, a matrix width, or a runner outside
# Actions entirely all work — the executor's whole interface is issue read/write
# plus the repo at HEAD.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
=== .github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml
# Claudinite work-item queue — the generator's scheduler run and its drain (tasks-dispatch
# DESIGN §5, §10). This is the repo's ONLY cron, and it replaces the slot
# scheduler's content at the same path when `taskScheduler.dispatch` is `"queue"`
# — same file, same hashed minute, different mechanism, so the one-cron rule and
# every reader that knows this workflow by name keep holding.
#
# A thin shim: all logic lives in the vendored engine, so this file changes
# rarely. The minute below is a placeholder; bootstrap and the wiring converge
# rewrite it to this repo's stable hashed minute in :10–:50, computed by
# `node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs <owner/repo>`.
#
# TWO JOBS, IN ORDER. The scheduler run is pure label mechanics over the issue list —
# instantiate each task's standing item at its anchor, ready what is due, reclaim
# dead executor claims — and evaluates no precondition and collects no signal. The
# drain then STARTS an executor run for what the scheduler run just created, which is what
# keeps the common case's latency at zero even with no `labeled` event delivered.
# Lost events are therefore never the only delivery — they are latency sugar,
# which is what retires the re-arm.
#
# The drain dispatches rather than executes, and that is the point: this workflow's
# concurrency group serializes SCHEDULER RUNS, and an executor run inside it would make each
# hour's scheduler run queue behind the previous hour's work — which the heartbeat, by making
# long work legal, turned from theoretical into likely (DESIGN §15.16).
#
# `workflow_dispatch` is not a convenience: it is the never-wait-for-the-cron

input.title: Adoption leaves the queue's agent hop unwired — no routine, no taskScheduler.endpoints, and no handover
input.body:
Adopting Claudinite on a fresh member lands the scheduler and executor workflows, the task declarations and the queue, but nothing in the adoption flow creates the member's invocation routine or declares `taskScheduler.endpoints`. The result is a member that looks fully adopted and drains only its code-work tasks — every task with an agentic phase fails at the hand-off:

> Could not start an agent session: this repo's config declares no invocation endpoint "default" (taskScheduler.endpoints)

Seen on `missingbulb/WIP`, adopted 2026-08-20: four work items (missingbulb/WIP#12, missingbulb/WIP#20, missingbulb/WIP#24, missingbulb/WIP#27) were claimed, handed off, refused, and labelled `needs-human` before anyone looked. The code-work-only tasks completed normally, so the queue's own signals all read healthy.

Two distinct gaps, and the second is the one that let it sit unnoticed for a day:

1. **`adopt-claudinite` never wires the endpoint.** It asks no adoption question about invocation, writes no `taskScheduler.endpoints` entry, and names no secret — so `resolveEndpoint` fails on the very first agentic item of a new member's life. Either the skill should walk the operator through creating the routine and declaring the endpoint, or a member with no endpoint should fail loudly at adoption time rather than at the first hand-off.
2. **No handover issue is filed for the part a human must do.** The routine's API token and the repo Actions secret are human-only steps, and the canon's own rule is that such a step gets its own issue with a checkbox per step and what breaks while each is off. Adoption files nothing — the gap exists only as three bot comments on a dead work item, which is exactly where nobody reads it.

Worth deciding alongside this: whether a per-member routine is the intended shape at all, or whether adoption should point new members at the fleet routine by default and let a member opt into its own.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
